items.title: Fork
items.text: A fork is a single move that attacks two or more enemy pieces at once, so the opponent can usually save only one of them. Check that the forking piece cannot simply be captured.

items.title: Pin
items.text: A pin freezes a piece because moving it would expose a more valuable piece (or the king) behind it on the same line. A pinned piece is a good target for extra attackers.

items.title: Skewer
items.text: A skewer attacks a valuable piece that must move, exposing a less valuable piece behind it on the same line.

items.title: Discovered attack
items.text: Moving one piece can uncover an attack by a piece behind it. If the uncovered attack is a check, the moving piece may make a second threat at the same time.

items.title: Hanging pieces
items.text: A piece is hanging when the opponent can win it by capture without adequate compensation. Before every move, check which of your pieces are attacked and whether each is sufficiently defended.

items.title: Back-rank weakness
items.text: A king with no flight squares because its own pieces block the squares in front of it can be mated by a rook or queen on the back rank. Creating an escape square (luft) removes the weakness.

items.title: Overloaded piece
items.text: A piece that is the only defender of two things cannot do both jobs; forcing it to capture or move can win material.

items.title: Trapped piece
items.text: A piece that is attacked and has no safe square can be lost even if it looks safe. Edge pieces are especially prone to being trapped.

items.title: Mate threats
items.text: Always ask whether the opponent has a checkmating move if you make a non-forcing move, and whether you have one yourself.

items.title: Opening principles
items.text: In the opening, develop minor pieces, fight for the centre, castle to safety, and avoid moving the same piece repeatedly or starting an attack before development is complete.

items.title: King safety
items.text: Pawns in front of the king and nearby defenders form its shelter. Advancing those pawns weakens the shelter, so do it only when the attack justifies it.

items.title: Pawn structure
items.text: Doubled and isolated pawns are structural weaknesses because they are harder to defend. Pawn moves cannot be undone, so consider what squares a pawn move gives up.

items.title: Piece activity
items.text: Improve your least active piece before committing to a plan; active pieces control more squares and create more threats.

items.title: Endgame activity
items.text: In endgames the king becomes an active piece, and rooks belong behind passed pawns and on active files.

items.title: Calculation checklist
items.text: Before moving, list checks, captures and threats for both sides, then verify your intended line one forcing reply at a time.
